Chest tightness in a 72-year-old six weeks after a major bereavement should not be attributed to grief without medical assessment; if it is happening now, is severe or persistent, or comes with breathlessness, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to the arm, back, jaw, or neck, call emergency services. Grief can produce real bodily changes: activation of the stress system can raise heart rate, blood pressure, stress hormones, and blood clotting, increasing cardiovascular strain. The highest reported excess heart-attack risk is immediately after a death—about 21 times higher on the first day and six times higher during the first week—and cardiovascular risk can remain relevant during the first few months. Severe emotional stress can also trigger stress cardiomyopathy, sometimes called “broken-heart syndrome,” which may resemble a heart attack and cannot safely be distinguished from one at home. In older people with coronary plaque, a sudden rise in heart rate and blood pressure may increase mechanical stress on a plaque and contribute to a cardiovascular event. Grief may dysregulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, increasing cortisol and contributing to disturbed sleep, reduced appetite, and difficulty concentrating. Stress-related cortisol changes can also affect immune functioning, with prolonged stress associated with greater susceptibility to infection and with inflammatory illnesses, although this does not mean that every bereaved person will become immunologically ill. Inflammation is a normal part of immune defence, but prolonged stress-related inflammation may be harmful and has been linked with cardiovascular and other chronic diseases. At six weeks, poor sleep, low appetite, sadness, and fluctuating functioning can still be part of normal mourning, because bereavement has no single correct emotional pattern or duration. Those symptoms still deserve attention when they impair eating, hydration, medication-taking, sleep, safety, or daily functioning, because physical deterioration can become a medical problem even when the underlying grief is normal. Arrange a prompt appointment with her general practitioner or usual doctor to review the chest symptoms, blood pressure, pulse, medication list and missed doses, sleep, food and fluid intake, and any new breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness, or falls. She should not restart, stop, double, or otherwise alter blood-pressure medication without advice from her prescriber, and a family member can respectfully help with a pill organiser, reminders, repeat prescriptions, transport, and meals if she agrees. The clinician may decide that an examination, blood-pressure readings, an electrocardiogram, blood tests, or other cardiac investigations are appropriate; the important point is to assess her symptoms rather than presume their cause. Support can be offered without labelling her grief abnormal: listen, acknowledge that grief affects bodies as well as feelings, offer company for appointments and meals, encourage gentle routine and hydration, and ask whether she would welcome a bereavement counsellor, psychologist, grief group, or faith/community support. Avoid assuming that chest tightness is “only emotional,” that a normal grief reaction cannot coexist with a heart attack, that a heart-related cause would disprove her grief, or that one difficult six-week period means she has a psychiatric disorder. Also avoid assuming that a single cortisol, inflammation, or immune test can measure the seriousness of her grief, or that supplements, sedatives, alcohol, or borrowed medicines are safe solutions. Professional grief assessment becomes particularly important if distress remains overwhelming or disabling without improvement, or around 12 months after the death if persistent yearning or inability to accept the loss is accompanied by marked impairment and symptoms such as withdrawal, bitterness, identity disruption, or inability to resume life. Any talk of wanting to die, inability to stay safe, severe confusion, or inability to eat, drink, or take essential medicines warrants urgent professional help rather than waiting for grief to resolve on its own.

Chest tightness in a 72-year-old six weeks after a major bereavement should not be attributed to grief without medical assessment; if it is happening now, is severe or persistent, or comes with breathlessness, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to the arm, back, jaw, or neck, call emergency services. [shard_05790_56499] [shard_01402_2476]

Grief can produce real bodily changes: activation of the stress system can raise heart rate, blood pressure, stress hormones, and blood clotting, increasing cardiovascular strain. [shard_05790_56499] [shard_00700_42769]

The highest reported excess heart-attack risk is immediately after a death—about 21 times higher on the first day and six times higher during the first week—and cardiovascular risk can remain relevant during the first few months. [shard_05790_56499] [shard_00700_42769]

Severe emotional stress can also trigger stress cardiomyopathy, sometimes called “broken-heart syndrome,” which may resemble a heart attack and cannot safely be distinguished from one at home. [shard_00653_31512] [shard_01402_2476]

In older people with coronary plaque, a sudden rise in heart rate and blood pressure may increase mechanical stress on a plaque and contribute to a cardiovascular event. [shard_04241_81034]

Grief may dysregulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, increasing cortisol and contributing to disturbed sleep, reduced appetite, and difficulty concentrating. [shard_06255_38667]

Stress-related cortisol changes can also affect immune functioning, with prolonged stress associated with greater susceptibility to infection and with inflammatory illnesses, although this does not mean that every bereaved person will become immunologically ill. [shard_01181_80440]

Inflammation is a normal part of immune defence, but prolonged stress-related inflammation may be harmful and has been linked with cardiovascular and other chronic diseases. [shard_06035_68554]

At six weeks, poor sleep, low appetite, sadness, and fluctuating functioning can still be part of normal mourning, because bereavement has no single correct emotional pattern or duration. [shard_06425_9522]

Those symptoms still deserve attention when they impair eating, hydration, medication-taking, sleep, safety, or daily functioning, because physical deterioration can become a medical problem even when the underlying grief is normal. [shard_05790_56499] [shard_04366_29939]

Arrange a prompt appointment with her general practitioner or usual doctor to review the chest symptoms, blood pressure, pulse, medication list and missed doses, sleep, food and fluid intake, and any new breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness, or falls. [shard_05790_56499] [shard_00700_42769]

She should not restart, stop, double, or otherwise alter blood-pressure medication without advice from her prescriber, and a family member can respectfully help with a pill organiser, reminders, repeat prescriptions, transport, and meals if she agrees. [shard_05790_56499]

The clinician may decide that an examination, blood-pressure readings, an electrocardiogram, blood tests, or other cardiac investigations are appropriate; the important point is to assess her symptoms rather than presume their cause.

Support can be offered without labelling her grief abnormal: listen, acknowledge that grief affects bodies as well as feelings, offer company for appointments and meals, encourage gentle routine and hydration, and ask whether she would welcome a bereavement counsellor, psychologist, grief group, or faith/community support. [shard_04491_66399] [shard_04366_29939]

Avoid assuming that chest tightness is “only emotional,” that a normal grief reaction cannot coexist with a heart attack, that a heart-related cause would disprove her grief, or that one difficult six-week period means she has a psychiatric disorder. [shard_01402_2476] [shard_06425_9522]

Also avoid assuming that a single cortisol, inflammation, or immune test can measure the seriousness of her grief, or that supplements, sedatives, alcohol, or borrowed medicines are safe solutions.

Professional grief assessment becomes particularly important if distress remains overwhelming or disabling without improvement, or around 12 months after the death if persistent yearning or inability to accept the loss is accompanied by marked impairment and symptoms such as withdrawal, bitterness, identity disruption, or inability to resume life. [shard_04366_29939] [shard_05326_55859]

Any talk of wanting to die, inability to stay safe, severe confusion, or inability to eat, drink, or take essential medicines warrants urgent professional help rather than waiting for grief to resolve on its own. [shard_04366_29939]
